statement: In a nationally representative US survey of 202,248 adults aged 25 or older (113,752 women and 88,496 men, interviewed in 1997 to 2004 and followed through death records for about 7 years on average, to the end of 2006), people who currently smoked cigarettes compared with people who had smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in their lives died at about three times the rate at ages 25 to 79 (adjusted hazard ratio 3.0 in women, 99% CI 2.7 to 3.3; 2.8 in men, 2.4 to 3.1). The ratio was largest for lung cancer (17.8 in women, 14.6 in men) and respiratory disease (8.5 and 9.0), about 3 for ischemic heart disease (3.5 and 3.2) and for stroke in women (3.2), and 1.7 for stroke in men, with an interval from 1.0 to 2.8. The authors estimate that about 6 in 10 of the deaths among people who currently smoked at these ages (62% in women, 60% in men) would have been avoided if their death rates from disease had matched those of people who never smoked. Scaled to US death rates for 2004, they estimate that 38 in 100 women and 26 in 100 men who currently smoked would survive from age 25 to 80, against 70 in 100 women and 61 in 100 men who never smoked, a difference of about 11 and 12 years of life. Compared with people who continued to smoke, people who had stopped gained about 10, 9, 6 and 4 years of life when they stopped at 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 years of age (read from survival curves). Those who stopped at 35 to 44 (median 39) still had 1.2 times the death rate of people who never smoked, against 3.0 for people who continued: the authors read this as an excess cut by about 90% and call the remaining excess substantial (about 1 in 6 of such people who died before 80 would not have died at the rate of people who never smoked). These are averages for groups, not what any one person would gain, and they concern cigarette smoking only. Smoking was recorded once, at the interview, so people who stopped afterwards stay in the smoking group; the amount smoked, other tobacco products, vapes and pouches were not examined; adjustment covered age, education, alcohol and body-mass index but not diet, physical activity or income; and the paper does not show the authors' checks of what adjustment, national scaling and leaving out the first two years of follow-up changed. The US Surgeon General's 2014 report, as summarized in its listed conclusions, judges the evidence sufficient to infer that cigarette smoking increases the risk of death from any cause in men and women and that it is the dominant cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and states that cigarette smoking is causally linked to disease in nearly all organs; those listed conclusions give no change in the risk of death or of the main diseases after stopping, apart from a better prognosis for people with cancer and, graded suggestive but not sufficient, a lower risk of advanced age-related macular degeneration. The cohort study was funded by the US National Institutes of Health (Fogarty International Center), the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Gates Foundation's Disease Control Priorities Project; no tobacco-industry funding is printed. Certainty: moderate. Status: single study.
population: US adults aged 25 or older in the National Health Interview Survey, interviewed 1997 to 2004 (113,752 women and 88,496 men analysed; 15,715 deaths to the end of 2006; mean follow-up about 7 years)
exposure: Currently smoking cigarettes at the interview (23,839 women and 23,348 men), counting people who stopped within 5 years before death as still smoking; stopping at 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54 or 55 to 64 years of age (medians 29, 39, 49 and 59)
comparator: Having smoked fewer than 100 cigarettes in a lifetime (67,524 women and 39,289 men); for stopping, people who continued to smoke
outcome: Death from any cause and from lung cancer, ischemic heart disease, stroke, respiratory disease and other causes at ages 25 to 79; modelled probability of surviving from age 25 to 80; years of life gained by stopping
magnitude: Adjusted hazard ratios (99% CI), current smoking against never smoking, ages 25 to 79, women / men: all causes 3.0 (2.7 to 3.3) / 2.8 (2.4 to 3.1); lung cancer 17.8 (11.4 to 27.8) / 14.6 (9.1 to 23.4); ischemic heart disease 3.5 (2.7 to 4.6) / 3.2 (2.5 to 4.1); stroke 3.2 (2.2 to 4.7) / 1.7 (1.0 to 2.8); respiratory disease 8.5 (6.1 to 11.8) / 9.0 (5.6 to 14.4); all cancers 3.2 (2.6 to 3.9) / 3.8 (3.1 to 4.8). Deaths from any cause in the never-smoked and current groups: 2,190 and 1,579 in women, 1,283 and 2,030 in men; all-cause ratios 3.1 and 2.8 after excluding people who stopped within 5 years before death and people with earlier heart disease, stroke or cancer. Share of deaths among people who currently smoked that would have been avoided at never-smoked disease death rates: 62% (59 to 65) in women and 60% (55 to 63) in men (accidents and injuries, about 7% of the excess, not counted). Probability of surviving from 25 to 80, scaled to 2004 US death rates, never smoked against currently smoking: women 70% (99% CI 64 to 76) against 38% (30 to 45); men 61% (55 to 67) against 26% (18 to 33); gaps of 32 and 35 percentage points (editors' subtraction) and about 11 and 12 years. Stopping against continuing to smoke: about 10, 9, 6 and 4 years of life gained at 25 to 34, 35 to 44, 45 to 54 and 55 to 64 (no intervals given in the text); hazard ratio 1.2 for those who stopped at 35 to 44 against people who never smoked, 3.0 for those who continued (excess of 0.2 against 2.0, about 90% less, editors' arithmetic); excess cut by about two thirds for stopping at 45 to 54.

evidence.locator: Methods › Study Design, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Results › Mortality According to Smoking Status, 1st paragraph
evidence.extracted: National Health Interview Survey adults interviewed 1997 to 2004 and linked to the National Death Index to 31 December 2006 (match success above 95%): 216,917 aged 25 or older, of whom 14,669 were dropped for a missing variable (9,058 women, 5,611 men), leaving 113,752 women and 88,496 men; mean follow-up 7 years (1.3 million person-years); 15,715 deaths (8,236 in women, 7,479 in men), 10,743 of them at ages 25 to 79. The sampling frame leaves out about 7 million of 226 million US adults (long-term care, prison, active-duty military); Black and Hispanic people are oversampled and weighted back to national proportions.
evidence.source_read: publisher full text (HTML), NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128 (Supplementary Appendix and disclosure forms, both PDFs, not opened)

evidence.extracted: Never smoked: fewer than 100 cigarettes in a lifetime. People who had stopped smoking: at least 100 cigarettes in a lifetime and none in the previous 5 years. People who had stopped within 5 years before death were counted as currently smoking, the authors' step against reverse causation. Age-stratified Cox models adjusted for education (3 levels), alcohol (4 levels) and body-mass index (3 levels), weighted to the survey; adding race made no material difference (not presented). Survival from 25 to 80 combines age-specific ratios, smoking prevalence and 2004 US death rates; scaling the survey's death rates up to national rates did not materially change the absolute differences (data not shown).

By cause, women / men: lung cancer 94% / 93% of deaths, ischemic heart disease 72% / 69%, respiratory disease 88% / 89%.

evidence.extracted: Probability of surviving from age 25 to 80 (scaled to 2004 US death rates; the Results sentence lists adjustment for age, education and body-mass index, the Methods also list alcohol): women 70% (99% CI 64 to 76) if never smoked against 38% (30 to 45) if currently smoking; men 61% (55 to 67) against 26% (18 to 33); survival shorter by about 11 years in women and 12 in men. The authors say the gap at age 80 now exceeds 30 percentage points in both sexes (32 and 35 from the printed figures, editors' subtraction).

evidence.locator: Results › Benefits of Smoking Cessation, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figures 3 and 4
evidence.extracted: Compared with continuing to smoke, stopping at 25 to 34 (median 29) gave survival nearly the same as never smoking, about 10 years of life gained; at 35 to 44 (median 39) about 9 years, with a hazard ratio of 1.2 against people who never smoked, against 3.0 for people who continued (excess cut by about 90%); at 45 to 54 about 6 years, excess cut by about two thirds; at 55 to 64 about 4 years. Figure 4 is cited for the ratios of 1.2 and 3.0; the ratios for the other ages at stopping are shown there and in the Supplementary Appendix (not opened) and are not used here. People may have stopped because of illness, which would overstate the risk in the group that stopped; leaving out the first 2 years of follow-up left the results similar (data not shown).
evidence.source_read: publisher full text (HTML), NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128 (Supplementary Appendix and disclosure forms, both PDFs, not opened)

evidence.extracted: The authors say that stopping at around 40 cuts the excess risk of death by about 90%, but that the remaining excess of about 20% (hazard ratio 1.2) is substantial: about 1 in 6 of the people who had stopped and who die before 80 would not have died at the death rates of people of similar education, adiposity and alcohol use who never smoked. They add that the absolute benefits of stopping are large because the absolute risks of continuing are large.
evidence.source_read: publisher full text (HTML), NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128 (Supplementary Appendix and disclosure forms, both PDFs, not opened)

evidence.extracted: The authors describe the tripling of the relative risk of death and the loss of at least a decade as similar to four other studies (male British doctors born 1900 to 1930, a UK women's study, a meta-analysis of other US cohorts and a study in Japan); the risks for the women are about 50% greater than in studies from the 1980s; absolute death rates are higher than in other US studies because the survey is more representative. Those four studies were not read.
evidence.source_read: publisher full text (HTML), NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128 (Supplementary Appendix and disclosure forms, both PDFs, not opened)

evidence.extracted: Limits the authors state: confounders other than the few recorded (adjustment did little to the ratios, which they read as suggesting the association is to a large degree causal); people in prison are outside the survey; fewer deaths than in recent studies; causes of death may be misclassified at older ages (not affecting all-cause ratios); smoking was measured only at the start, so some people who currently smoked later stopped (any distortion slight over 7 years); the excess among people who had stopped may be overstated because some stopped when ill; little difference was found in alcohol use, adiposity and other health variables between people who stopped and people who never smoked.
evidence.source_read: publisher full text (HTML), NEJM, https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMsa1211128 (Supplementary Appendix and disclosure forms, both PDFs, not opened)

evidence.locator: Chapter 1 › Chapter Conclusions › Chapter 11, conclusions 1 to 3; Chapter 7 › Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, conclusion 1; Major Conclusions, conclusion 3
evidence.extracted: Graded by the report as sufficient to infer a causal relationship: cigarette smoking increases the risk of death from any cause in men and women, smoking causes diminished overall health, and the relative risk of dying from cigarette smoking has risen over the last 50 years in US men and women (chapter 11, conclusions 1 to 3); smoking is the dominant cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in men and women in the US and causes all elements of it (chapter 7, conclusion 1). Major conclusion 3 states that cigarette smoking has been causally linked to disease in nearly all organs, to diminished health status and to harm to the fetus.

evidence.extracted: Stopping, as far as the chapter conclusions are listed in chapter 1: quitting is said to improve the prognosis of people with cancer (chapter 6, conclusion 1, within a conclusion graded sufficient for the link between smoking and adverse outcomes in cancer patients), and the report grades as suggestive but not sufficient that stopping reduces the risk of advanced age-related macular degeneration (chapter 10). No listed conclusion gives the change in the risk of death or of the main diseases after stopping; the report's chapters on stopping and treatment were not read.

evidence.extracted: How the report's judgments are made: four levels (sufficient to infer a causal relationship; suggestive but not sufficient; inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship; suggestive of no causal relationship) from a synthesis of all the evidence on consistency, strength, specificity, temporality and coherence; chapters written by 75 experts and reviewed by more than 100 peer reviewers; no databases, dates or selection rules are stated for the evidence behind the conclusions used here, so the report is read as a narrative review.

risk_of_bias.note: The study card rates the cohort 'some concerns' on ROBINS-E: smoking self-reported once at the interview, four adjustment variables, and sensitivity analyses reported as data not shown. None is expected to account for a threefold all-cause ratio, and measuring smoking once, with some people stopping later, pushes the ratios toward 1. Not downgraded.

inconsistency.note: One cohort was read; the authors describe four other studies as giving similar ratios (not read).

indirectness.note: The claim is restricted to the surveyed US adults, to cigarettes and to the outcomes measured. The 2014 report's conclusions are second-hand and are used as context, not for any figure.

imprecision.note: Intervals are narrow for all causes and the main causes; the stroke ratio in men (1.0 to 2.8) and the years-gained figures (no intervals given in the text) are less certain and are worded so.

large_effect.note: All-cause ratio about 3 with a lower limit of 2.4; lung cancer 15 to 18; the all-cause ratios stay at 3.1 and 2.8 after excluding recent quitters and people with earlier heart disease, stroke or cancer. The biases that remain (one baseline measurement, limited adjustment) are not expected to explain a ratio of this size, and the first runs toward 1.

dose_response.note: No ratio by amount smoked is printed in the paper, so no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational (a national survey linked to death records), so it starts low. Upgraded one level for a large effect: the all-cause ratio is about 3 (lower limit 2.4) and the lung cancer ratios are 15 to 18, they stay at 3.1 and 2.8 in the printed sensitivity analysis, and the biases that remain (smoking measured once, which pushes toward 1; four adjustment variables; cause-of-death misclassification, which does not touch the all-cause ratios) are not expected to produce a ratio of this size. Not downgraded for risk of bias (ROBINS-E: some concerns, none likely to account for a threefold ratio); read strictly, without the upgrade, the rating would be low. The rating applies to the all-cause, lung cancer, respiratory and heart disease ratios and to the survival figures; the stroke ratio in men (1.7, interval 1.0 to 2.8), the years of life gained by stopping (read from survival curves, with no intervals given in the text; the all-cause ratios for people who had stopped are in a supplementary table that was not opened) and the 90% figure (measured for one age group) are less certain, taken alone they would be rated low, and the statement words them so. The Surgeon General's 2014 conclusions are second-hand (a narrative review with no stated search) and are used for context only. Status single study because only the survey cohort was read: Jha et al. describe four other prospective studies as giving similar ratios, and reading them could move the status to replicated. The survey is run by a US federal agency and the analysis was funded by public bodies and a charitable foundation; no industry funding is printed (the disclosure forms were not opened).

verification.flag_note: Draft for section 7 by the co-editor (decision p-ways-of-taking): held off the site until the senior author approves this version. Status single study because only the NHIS cohort was read. Jha et al. describe four other prospective studies as giving similar ratios; none has a reference record or study card here: Doll et al. 2004, BMJ (doi 10.1136/bmj.38142.554479.AE); Pirie et al. 2012, Lancet (doi 10.1016/S0140-6736(12)61720-6); Sakata et al. 2012, BMJ (doi 10.1136/bmj.e7093); Thun et al. 2013, NEJM (doi 10.1056/NEJMsa1211127). Reading them would let the editors move the status to replicated. The Supplementary Appendix (Tables S1 to S3) and the disclosure forms (PDFs) were not opened; the all-cause hazard ratios for people who had stopped are in Table S2. Two of the authors work at US federal agencies (the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention), recorded on the study card; no industry funding is printed.
